learn.title: Arrays versus lists
learn.body: An array gives instant access to item i, and its items sit together in memory. A list cannot jump: to reach the tenth node you walk nine steps. In return, a list can insert at the front without moving anything, and it grows one node at a time.

learn.title: The price of a pointer
learn.body: Each node stores a pointer as well as its value. On a typical 64-bit machine a node holding an int takes 16 bytes, where the int alone is 4. Small separate allocations also cost time. Lists win when you add and remove a lot, not when you read by position.

learn.title: Looking both ways
learn.body: A doubly linked node also points back. You can walk in both directions and unlink a node without searching for its predecessor.

learn.title: Unlinking a middle node
learn.body: Given a node p with neighbours on both sides, no walk is needed.

learn.title: Which one?
learn.body: A playlist where songs are often added, removed in the middle and played in order.
steps: Random access by index is rare, so an array's main strength is unused
Removal in the middle is frequent, which pointers handle cheaply
A doubly linked list also lets the user go to the previous song

questions.prompt: What is a clear strength of an array over a linked list?
choices: Growing one node at a time
questions.explanation: An array can jump to a position by arithmetic. A list must walk.

questions.prompt: What does a doubly linked node add?
choices: A pointer to the previous node
questions.explanation: With `prev`, you can walk backwards and unlink a node you already hold.

questions.prompt: A node has an int and one pointer, 16 bytes in total on a typical 64-bit machine. How many bytes is the int alone?
questions.explanation: An int is 4 bytes. The pointer takes 8 and padding fills the rest.

questions.prompt: Which job suits a linked list best?
choices: Storing a fixed table of 12 items
Many insertions and removals at the front
questions.explanation: Front insertion and removal change only a pointer or two.

questions.prompt: To unlink node p in a doubly linked list, set p->prev->next to p->\_\_.
questions.explanation: The earlier node must skip p and point to the node after it.

questions.prompt: Match each need to the better fit.
questions.explanation: Arrays are compact and indexed. Lists trade space and speed of reading for easy insertion.

questions.prompt: A doubly linked list costs more than a singly linked one in...
choices: memory per node and pointers to update
questions.explanation: Every node carries an extra pointer, and every insert or delete updates more links.
